subChunks.title: For Loops
subChunks.hookHtml: Imagine you need to print the numbers 1 through 100. Would you really write System.out.println(1); one hundred times? There is a much better way — the for loop.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The For Loop

A for loop repeats a block of code a controlled number of times. It has three parts separated by semicolons:

for (initialisation; condition; update) {
    // code to repeat
}
  1. Initialisation — runs once before the loop starts, e.g. int i = 1
  2. Condition — checked before every iteration; the loop continues while it is true
  3. Update — runs after every iteration, e.g. i++ to increment the counter
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

This prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The counter i starts at 1, keeps going while i <= 5, and increases by 1 each time (i++).

Counting down — just flip the logic:

for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Off-by-one pitfall — using i < 5 instead of i <= 5 prints 1–4, not 1–5. Always double-check your boundary condition!

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin unrolls a long scroll covered in identical runes — the same symbol repeated one hundred times.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A foolish apprentice once spent three days copying this repetition scroll by hand. There is a better way. We call it the repetition incantation — or, in Java, the for loop.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A for loop has three sacred runes: where to start, when to stop, and how to step forward each time.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Magnificent! Five lines of output from three lines of code. Beware the off-by-one curse — if you write i < 5 instead of i <= 5, the loop stops one step too early!

questions.questionHtml: Which part of a for loop runs exactly once, before the loop starts?
questions.explanationHtml: The initialisation (e.g. int i = 0) runs once before the first iteration. The condition is checked before each iteration, and the update runs after each iteration.

questions.questionHtml: for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++) will print the number 5 if you put System.out.println(i) inside the loop body.
questions.explanationHtml: The condition i < 5 stops the loop when i equals 5 — so 5 is never printed. Use i <= 5 to include 5.

questions.questionHtml:
Fill in the blank to make this loop count from 1 to 100:
for (int i = 1; ______; i++) { ... }
questions.explanationHtml: The condition i <= 100 keeps the loop running while i is at most 100, so all values 1–100 are included.

questions.questionHtml: This loop is supposed to count from 10 down to 1. What is wrong?
questions.explanationHtml: The update i++ increases i each iteration, so the loop runs forever (infinite loop). To count down, use i--.

subChunks.title: While Loops
subChunks.hookHtml: Sometimes you don't know how many times a loop should run — you just know the condition that should stop it. That is exactly what the while loop is for.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The While Loop

A while loop keeps running as long as its condition is true:

while (condition) {
    // code to repeat
}

The condition is checked before each iteration. If it is false the very first time, the body never runs.

int count = 1;
while (count <= 3) {
    System.out.println("Count: " + count);
    count++;
}

Infinite loop danger — if you forget to update the variable inside the loop, the condition never becomes false and the program hangs forever.

do-while variant — the body runs at least once before the condition is checked:

int x = 10;
do {
    System.out.println(x);
    x--;
} while (x > 5);

When to use while vs for? — Use for when you know the number of iterations in advance. Use while when you only know the stopping condition.

storyBeats.text: In the Academy courtyard, a stone golem patrols endlessly — until its enchantment runs out.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice the golem, young apprentice. It does not patrol a fixed number of steps — it patrols until its energy is depleted. That is the essence of a while loop.

storyBeats.speaker: The patrolling golem
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The loop checks energy > 0 before each patrol. When energy reaches zero, the golem stops. But if you forget energy-- inside the loop... the golem walks forever. That is an infinite loop — a dangerous curse indeed!

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, use a while loop to print every third number from 3 up to 30 (i.e. 3, 6, 9 … 30), each on its own line. After the loop, print Done!.

questions.questionHtml: When is the condition of a while loop checked?
questions.explanationHtml: The while loop checks its condition before each iteration. If the condition is false from the start, the body never runs.

questions.questionHtml: A do-while loop is guaranteed to execute its body at least once.
questions.explanationHtml: do-while runs the body first, then checks the condition. So the body always executes at least once, even if the condition is false initially.
n starts at 1 (prints), then becomes 3 (prints), then becomes 5 which is not < 4, so the loop ends.

questions.questionHtml: Which scenario is best handled by a while loop rather than a for loop?
options: Keep reading user input until they type 'quit'
Print every element in a fixed-size array
questions.correctAnswer: Keep reading user input until they type 'quit'
questions.explanationHtml: When you don't know in advance how many iterations are needed — only the stopping condition — a while loop is the natural choice.

subChunks.title: Loop Control: break & continue
subChunks.hookHtml: What if you want to skip one specific iteration, or stop the loop entirely when something unexpected happens? break and continue give you precise control.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
break and continue

break — exits the entire loop immediately, regardless of the condition.

for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    if (i == 5) break; // stop when i reaches 5
    System.out.println(i);
}

This prints 1, 2, 3, 4 — the loop ends before 5 is ever printed.

continue — skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one.

for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
    if (i % 2 != 0) continue; // skip odd numbers
    System.out.println(i);
}

This prints 2, 4, 6 — odd numbers are skipped but the loop keeps going.

Nested loops — break and continue only affect the innermost loop they are inside. To break out of an outer loop, you can use labelled break: outerLoop: for (...) and then break outerLoop;.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin sits at a grand pipe organ, playing a magical melody. Certain notes must be skipped; others signal the end of the piece.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This musical spell has twelve notes. But certain dissonant notes — the odd ones — must be skipped, or the magic goes awry. And if I reach note eight, I must shatter the loop entirely before the spell spirals out of control.

storyBeats.speaker: Skipping notes with continue
Shattering the loop with break
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: continue merely hops over a single note and plays on. break ends the entire performance. Two very different powers — use them wisely!

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, loop from 1 to 50. Use continue to skip any number that is not a multiple of 7, and use break to stop after you have printed four multiples. Expected output: 7, 14, 21, 28.

questions.questionHtml: What does the break statement do inside a loop?
questions.explanationHtml: break immediately exits the loop — no more iterations occur. To skip just one iteration while keeping the loop going, use continue.
continue skips the rest of the loop body when i == 3, so 3 is never printed. The loop continues with 4 and 5.
break exits the loop entirely when i == 3. Only 1 and 2 are printed before that point.

questions.questionHtml: You want to search a list for a specific name and stop as soon as you find it. Which statement should you use?
questions.explanationHtml: break exits the loop the moment you find what you're looking for, making the search efficient. continue would only skip the current name and keep searching.

subChunks.title: Enhanced For & Nested Loops
subChunks.hookHtml: You've used the classic for loop with a counter. But when iterating over a collection, Java offers a cleaner syntax — and sometimes you need a loop inside a loop to handle grids and tables.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Enhanced For-Each Loop

The enhanced for loop (also called for-each) iterates over an array or collection without needing an index variable:

String[] spells = {"Fireball", "Frostbolt", "Thunder"};
for (String spell : spells) {
    System.out.println(spell);
}

Read the colon as "in" — "for each spell in spells".

Use for-each when: you don't need the index, you're not modifying the collection, and you want cleaner, less error-prone code.

Nested Loops

A loop inside another loop. The inner loop completes fully for each iteration of the outer loop:

for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {
    for (int col = 1; col <= 3; col++) {
        System.out.print(row * col + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

Performance note: if the outer loop runs N times and the inner loop runs M times, the total number of iterations is N × M. With large values this grows quickly — this is called O(N²) complexity.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin kneels before an ornate chest. Inside, row upon row of potion vials glimmer in the candlelight.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Sometimes we must examine every item in a collection, one by one. The for-each loop is the perfect incantation for this — elegant, unambiguous, impossible to mis-count.

storyBeats.speaker: Examining each potion
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But what if the chest is a grid — three rows, three columns? Then we need a loop within a loop — a nested incantation. Watch closely as I draw the star grid:

questions.questionHtml: What does the colon (:) mean in a for-each loop: for (String s : list)?
questions.explanationHtml: Read it as "for each s in list". The colon separates the loop variable from the collection being iterated.

questions.questionHtml: You can use a for-each loop to modify the original elements of a primitive array.
questions.explanationHtml: In a for-each loop, the loop variable is a copy of each element (for primitives). Modifying x in for (int x : arr) does not change the array. Use a regular indexed for loop to modify elements.
The outer loop runs 4 times, the inner loop runs 3 times per outer iteration: 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.questionHtml: Which loop type is best for iterating over all elements of a String[] without needing the index?
questions.explanationHtml: The enhanced for-each loop is cleaner and less error-prone when you only need the values, not the indices. It also works on any Iterable, not just arrays.
